Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval measured in seconds, let $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ be lengths in metres, and set $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with closure $\overline\Omega$. A rectangular local-equilibrium field record consists of an open temperature interval $\mathcal T\subset(0,\infty)$, a temperature field $T:\overline\Omega\times I\to\mathcal T$ whose time derivative through order one and spatial derivatives through order two extend continuously to $\overline\Omega\times I$, a function $u\in C^1(\mathcal T,\mathbb R)$ of internal-energy density in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and its volumetric heat capacity $c(T):=u'(T)>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$. The coordinates $x_i$ are lengths in metres, and $T$ is measured in kelvins, using [[def-td-si-quantities]].

The record may also include a heat-flux field $j_Q:\overline\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ with components in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and a conductivity field $K:\overline\Omega\times\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ with entries in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. The flux and tensor are field data here; no relation between them is imposed by this Definition. In Euclidean coordinates, $\nabla T=(\partial_{x_1}T,\partial_{x_2}T,\partial_{x_3}T)$ and $\operatorname{div}j_Q=\sum_i\partial_{x_i}(j_Q)_i$. On a flat face, $n$ denotes its outward unit normal.

This is a specified regular field class on a fixed rigid body. It does not assert that every physical medium has local-equilibrium fields, nor does it adopt a heat equation, a boundary condition, Fourier's law, or an entropy-production law.

For a field record on $\Omega\times I$ from [[def-td-rectangular-local-equilibrium-fields]], adopt the local balance
$$\partial_t u(T(x,t))+\operatorname{div}j_Q(x,t)=0$$
and the insulated-boundary condition $j_Q(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ on every face of $\partial\Omega$. Both terms in the local equation have units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$. The boundary condition says that no heat energy crosses the body's outer faces in this model.

This local continuum balance is an additional adopted postulate, with the sign and energy convention of [[post-td-first-law-energy]]. It is not deduced from that global process-record balance. Matter transfer, volume work, internal sources, moving boundaries, and external-field energy require separately specified balance models and are outside this item.

For the field record of [[def-td-rectangular-local-equilibrium-fields]], adopt
$$j_Q(x,t)=-K(x,T(x,t))\nabla T(x,t).$$
Here $K$ has entries in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and $j_Q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, so the equation is dimensionally consistent. Write $K_s=(K+K^{\mathsf T})/2$ for the symmetric part and assume $z^{\mathsf T}K_s(x,T)z\ge0$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^3$. The antisymmetric part may contribute to the flux but not to the quadratic entropy production.

This is an adopted constitutive model in the stated continuum regime. It is neither a consequence of equilibrium entropy alone nor a universal law for all media. In particular, it does not assert a finite propagation speed or an empirical value for $K$.

For the local-equilibrium medium of [[def-td-rectangular-local-equilibrium-fields]], adopt a local entropy density $s(T)$ measured in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$ with
$$\frac{ds}{dT}(T)=\frac{c(T)}{T},$$
where $c(T)=u'(T)>0$ is the volumetric heat capacity and $T>0$ is measured in kelvins. Equivalently, for a fixed reference $T_{\rm ref}>0$ and reference density $s_{\rm ref}$, set
$$s(T)=s_{\rm ref}+\int_{T_{\rm ref}}^T\frac{c(\theta)}{\theta}\,d\theta.$$
The volume integral of this field is the entropy assigned by this continuum model. This adopts a local thermodynamic relation extending the macroscopic entropy framework of [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]; it does not prove that every evolving medium has such a local entropy density or identify it with an arbitrary finite-system entropy function.

For constant $c(T)=c_0>0$, the adopted relation gives $s(T)=s_{\rm ref}+c_0\log(T/T_{\rm ref})$. This is a restricted constitutive specialization, not a universal equation of state.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

derivations.claim: By [A3] and the chain rule, $\partial_t s(T)=s'(T)\partial_tT=(c(T)/T)\partial_tT=(\partial_tu)/T$, since $u'(T)=c(T)$.

Substituting $j_Q=-K
abla T$ from [A2] makes the right side $(
abla T)^{\mathsf T}K
abla T/T^2$. For any real vector $z$, $z^{\mathsf T}Kz=z^{\mathsf T}K_sz$ because the scalar $z^{\mathsf T}(K-K^{\mathsf T})z$ equals its own negative; hence [A2] and $T>0$ make this quantity nonnegative.

For each coordinate $i$, apply [F2] to the $i$th component of $j_Q/T$ on $[0,L_i]$: its integral is the endpoint difference $[(j_Q)_i/T]_{x_i=0}^{x_i=L_i}$. By [F3] these one-dimensional integrals may be integrated over the other two coordinates and summed. The result is $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}(j_Q/T)\,dx=0$ because $j_Q\cdot n=0$ on every face and $T>0$. The same calculation gives $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}j_Q\,dx=0$.

The coordinate product rule and $
abla(1/T)=-
abla T/T^2$ give $\operatorname{div}(j_Q/T)=(\operatorname{div}j_Q)/T-j_Q\cdot
abla T/T^2$. Substituting [A1] and step 1.1 yields $\partial_t s(T)+\operatorname{div}(j_Q/T)=-j_Q\cdot
abla T/T^2$.

On $\overline\Omega\times[t_0,t_1]$, $\partial_t s(T)$ and $\partial_tu(T)$ are continuous. The one-dimensional fundamental theorem [F2] expresses each time difference quotient as the average of its continuous time derivative; uniform continuity on this compact set makes those quotients converge uniformly in $x$. Therefore differentiation passes through the bounded-box integrals. Integrating the local balance in step 2.1 and using the zero face integral in step 1.3 gives $S'(t)=\int_\Omega (\nabla T)^{\mathsf T}K_s\nabla T/T^2\,dx$. Its integrand is nonnegative by step 1.2. Integrating [A1] and using step 1.3 gives $\frac d{dt}\int_\Omega u(T)\,dx=0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For a field record on $\Omega\times I$ from [[def-td-rectangular-local-equilibrium-fields]], adopt the local balance
$$\partial_t u(T(x,t))+\operatorname{div}j_Q(x,t)=0$$
and the insulated-boundary condition $j_Q(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ on every face of $\partial\Omega$. Both terms in the local equation have units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$. The boundary condition says that no heat energy crosses the body's outer faces in this model.

This local continuum balance is an additional adopted postulate, with the sign and energy convention of [[post-td-first-law-energy]]. It is not deduced from that global process-record balance. Matter transfer, volume work, internal sources, moving boundaries, and external-field energy require separately specified balance models and are outside this item.

For the field record of [[def-td-rectangular-local-equilibrium-fields]], adopt
$$j_Q(x,t)=-K(x,T(x,t))\nabla T(x,t).$$
Here $K$ has entries in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and $j_Q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, so the equation is dimensionally consistent. Write $K_s=(K+K^{\mathsf T})/2$ for the symmetric part and assume $z^{\mathsf T}K_s(x,T)z\ge0$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^3$. The antisymmetric part may contribute to the flux but not to the quadratic entropy production.

This is an adopted constitutive model in the stated continuum regime. It is neither a consequence of equilibrium entropy alone nor a universal law for all media. In particular, it does not assert a finite propagation speed or an empirical value for $K$.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$, and let
$u_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and uniformly continuous. Define
$u(x,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t)u_0(y)\,dy$ for $t>0$ and
$u(x,0):=u_0(x)$. Then $u$ is $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$, satisfies $\partial_tu=\Delta_xu$ there, is
bounded with $\|u(\cdot,t)\|_\infty\le\|u_0\|_\infty$, and converges locally
uniformly at the initial time:
$\sup_{x\in K}|u(x,t)-u_0(x)|\to0$ as $t\downarrow0^+$ for every compact
$K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $t>0$: (i) $\Gamma(\cdot,t)>0$
and $\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x,t)\,dx=1$; (ii) parabolic scaling:
$\Gamma(\lambda x,\lambda^2t)=\lambda^{-n}\Gamma(x,t)$ for every $\lambda>0$ and
$x\in\mathbb R^n$; (iii) $\Gamma$ is $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$ and solves the heat equation there,
$\partial_t\Gamma(x,t)=\Delta_x\Gamma(x,t)$; (iv) for every multi-index $\alpha$
there is $C_{n,\alpha}<\infty$ with
$|D^\alpha_x\Gamma(x,t)|\le C_{n,\alpha}t^{-(|\alpha|+n)/2}e^{-|x|^2/(8t)}$ for
all $x\in\mathbb R^n$, $t>0$; in particular $\|\Gamma(\cdot,t)\|_1=1$ and
$(\Gamma(\cdot,t))_{t>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity on $\mathbb R^n$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ (bounded measurable data are included). The absolutely
convergent representative
$u(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t)f(y)\,dy$ is $C^\infty$ for $t>0$, and
for every multi-index $\alpha$ and $k\ge0$
$D_x^\alpha\partial_t^ku=(D_x^\alpha\partial_t^k\Gamma_t)*f$. Moreover
$|D_x^\alpha\partial_t^k\Gamma(x,t)|\le C_{n,\alpha,k}t^{-(n+|\alpha|+2k)/2}e^{-|x|^2/(8t)}$.
Domination is uniform on compact subsets $x\in K$, $\tau\le t\le T$ with
$0<\tau<T<\infty$; $u_t=\Delta u$.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be bounded and
continuous. Then for every compact set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$,

$$ \sup_{x \in K} |(f*K_\varepsilon)(x)-f(x)| \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+). $$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval measured in seconds, let $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ be lengths in metres, and set $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with closure $\overline\Omega$. A rectangular local-equilibrium field record consists of an open temperature interval $\mathcal T\subset(0,\infty)$, a temperature field $T:\overline\Omega\times I\to\mathcal T$ whose time derivative through order one and spatial derivatives through order two extend continuously to $\overline\Omega\times I$, a function $u\in C^1(\mathcal T,\mathbb R)$ of internal-energy density in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and its volumetric heat capacity $c(T):=u'(T)>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$. The coordinates $x_i$ are lengths in metres, and $T$ is measured in kelvins, using [[def-td-si-quantities]].

The record may also include a heat-flux field $j_Q:\overline\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ with components in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and a conductivity field $K:\overline\Omega\times\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ with entries in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. The flux and tensor are field data here; no relation between them is imposed by this Definition. In Euclidean coordinates, $\nabla T=(\partial_{x_1}T,\partial_{x_2}T,\partial_{x_3}T)$ and $\operatorname{div}j_Q=\sum_i\partial_{x_i}(j_Q)_i$. On a flat face, $n$ denotes its outward unit normal.

This is a specified regular field class on a fixed rigid body. It does not assert that every physical medium has local-equilibrium fields, nor does it adopt a heat equation, a boundary condition, Fourier's law, or an entropy-production law.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $n\ge1$ and $t>0$. The **heat kernel on $\mathbb R^n$** is the function

$$\Gamma(x,t):=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{|x|^2}{4t}\Bigr),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n,$$

where $|x|^2=\langle x,x\rangle$ is the Euclidean square of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $\exp$ is the real exponential function of
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]. For fixed $t>0$ the map
$x\mapsto\Gamma(x,t)$ is a composite of the quadratic form with the exponential
and a scalar multiple, so it is $C^\infty$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] by
[[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] and
[[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]], and it is
strictly positive by [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]. The
spatial Laplacian entering the heat equation is that of
[[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].

The **causal extension** of the heat kernel is $\Gamma(x,t)$ for $t>0$ and
$\Gamma(x,t):=0$ for $t\le0$; the displayed formula is not evaluated at $t=0$
as a function value. The normalisation is fixed by the unit-mass identity
proved for the kernel on this page, and the causal extension is used only as a
locally integrable function or, after embedding, as a distribution.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

derivations.claim: The assumptions on $g$ make it bounded and uniformly continuous, so [F1] applies. Write $U(x,\theta)=\Gamma_\theta*g(x)$ and set $T(x,t)=U(x,at)$. The chain rule gives $\partial_tT=aU_\theta(x,at)=a\Delta U(x,at)=a\Delta T$ for $t>0$; [F1] also gives the formula, smoothness, and local uniform initial convergence. Since $k=ac$, this is $c\partial_tT=k\Delta T$. With $u'(T)=c$, $u_t=cT_t$, and $j_Q=-k\nabla T$ from [A3, A4], the same equality gives $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}j_Q=c\partial_tT-k\Delta T=0$.

Positivity and unit mass in [F2] imply $T_{\min}\int\Gamma\le T(x,t)\le T_{\max}\int\Gamma$, hence $T_{\min}\le T\le T_{\max}$. Translation by $2L_i$ in the convolution variable preserves $g$ and Lebesgue measure by [F6], so $T$ is $2L_i$-periodic in $x_i$. Reflection $y_i\mapsto-y_i$ preserves Lebesgue measure by [F7] because its matrix has determinant of absolute value one; evenness of the kernel [F9] and of $g$ then makes $T$ even in each coordinate. For $t>0$, evenness gives $\partial_{x_i}T=0$ on the face $x_i=0$; periodicity gives $\partial_{x_i}T=\partial_{x_i}T$ at opposite faces $x_i=-L_i,L_i$, while evenness makes these two values negatives, so both vanish. The same boundary derivative holds at $t=0$ for $g$, and [A4] gives $j_Q\cdot n=0$ on every face.

By [F11], the stated $C^2$ hypothesis gives continuous derivatives through spatial order two. For $|\alpha|\le2$ and $t>0$, differentiating under the integral and then integrating by parts in each coordinate gives $D^\alpha T(x,t)=\int\Gamma(x-y,at)D^\alpha g(y)\,dy$. The products of kernel derivatives with bounded derivatives of $g$ are absolutely integrable by the Gaussian bound [F2], so [F10] licenses the iterated integrals; on each finite coordinate interval Newton–Leibniz [F8] gives the integration-by-parts identity, and the boundary terms vanish as the interval expands because of the Gaussian tails. Each $D^\alpha g$ is bounded and continuous, so [F4] makes this expression converge uniformly on $\overline\Omega$ to $D^\alpha g$ as $t\downarrow0$. Thus the spatial derivatives through order two extend continuously to the initial time.

For $t>0$, the heat equation and the same integration-by-parts argument give $\partial_tT(x,t)=a\int\Gamma(x-y,at)\Delta g(y)\,dy$. By [F4] this converges uniformly on $\overline\Omega$ to $a\Delta g(x)$. For $0<\varepsilon<t$, [F8] gives $T(x,t)-T(x,\varepsilon)=\int_\varepsilon^t\partial_sT(x,s)\,ds$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ is valid uniformly in $x$ by step 1.1 and the uniform limit just established; consequently $T(x,t)-g(x)=\int_0^t\partial_sT(x,s)\,ds$, and dividing by $t$ proves the right derivative $\partial_tT(x,0)=a\Delta g(x)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$ with $L_i>0$ metres, let $c>0$ be a constant volumetric heat capacity in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$ with $u'(T)=c$ throughout the range of $g$, let $k>0$ be a constant scalar conductivity in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ with $K\equiv kI_3$ in [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], and put $a=k/c$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$.

For $t>0$ define
$$T(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma(x-y,at)g(y)\,dy,\qquad \Gamma(z,\theta)=(4\pi\theta)^{-3/2}e^{-|z|^2/(4\theta)},$$
and set $T(x,0)=g(x)$ on $\overline\Omega$. This field is the unique $C^1$-in-time, $C^2$-in-space solution on each finite time interval of $c\partial_tT=k\Delta T$ on $\Omega$, with $\partial_nT=0$ on every face and the given initial value. It satisfies $T_{\min}\le T(x,t)\le T_{\max}$ for all $t\ge0$, has $C^2$ spatial derivatives continuous to $t=0$, and its right time derivative there is $a\Delta g$. Under [[post-td-local-energy-balance]] and [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], it is a global-in-time solution of that restricted physical continuum model.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$ with $L_i>0$ metres, let $c>0$ be a constant volumetric heat capacity in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$ with $u'(T)=c$ throughout the range of $g$, let $k>0$ be a constant scalar conductivity in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ with $K\equiv kI_3$ in [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], and put $a=k/c$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$.

For $t>0$ define
$$T(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma(x-y,at)g(y)\,dy,\qquad \Gamma(z,\theta)=(4\pi\theta)^{-3/2}e^{-|z|^2/(4\theta)},$$
and set $T(x,0)=g(x)$ on $\overline\Omega$. This field is the unique $C^1$-in-time, $C^2$-in-space solution on each finite time interval of $c\partial_tT=k\Delta T$ on $\Omega$, with $\partial_nT=0$ on every face and the given initial value. It satisfies $T_{\min}\le T(x,t)\le T_{\max}$ for all $t\ge0$, has $C^2$ spatial derivatives continuous to $t=0$, and its right time derivative there is $a\Delta g$. Under [[post-td-local-energy-balance]] and [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], it is a global-in-time solution of that restricted physical continuum model.

Let $d\ge1$, let $L_1,\ldots,L_d>0$, and let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^d(0,L_i)$. If $w\in C^1(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ has zero mean, then
$$\int_\Omega |w(x)|^2\,dx\le \frac d2\sum_{i=1}^d L_i^2\int_\Omega |\partial_iw(x)|^2\,dx\le C_\Omega\int_\Omega |\nabla w(x)|^2\,dx,$$
where $C_\Omega=\frac d2\max_iL_i^2$. All integrals are the multidimensional Riemann integrals of continuous functions on the indicated closed rectangles, with the usual extension to their interiors.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

derivations.claim: On each finite time interval the time derivative is continuous on the compact box, so its difference quotients converge uniformly under the spatial integral. By [F1] and [F4], coordinatewise application of [F3] gives $\overline T'(t)=aV^{-1}\int_\Omega\Delta T\,dx=0$: the integral of each second coordinate derivative is the difference of the corresponding first derivative on its two faces, and both normal derivatives vanish. Hence $\overline T(t)=\overline T(0)$.

Set $w(x,t)=T(x,t)-\overline T(0)$. Then [F4] and step 1.1 give $\int_\Omega w=0$, while $w_t=a\Delta w$ and $\partial_nw=0$. Differentiating $E(t)=\int_\Omega w^2$ and using [F4], the product rule, and [F3] in each coordinate gives $E'(t)=2a\int_\Omega w\Delta w=-2a\int_\Omega|\nabla w|^2$; each endpoint term is $w\partial_nw=0$.
Apply [F2] to $w(\cdot,t)$ in step 2.1. It gives $E(t)\le C_\Omega\int_\Omega|\nabla w|^2$, so $E'(t)\le-(2a/C_\Omega)E(t)$.

The product rule gives $(e^{2at/C_\Omega}E(t))'=e^{2at/C_\Omega}(E'(t)+(2a/C_\Omega)E(t))\le0$ by step 3.1. Integrating this derivative with [F3] from $0$ to $t$ yields $e^{2at/C_\Omega}E(t)\le E(0)$, which is the asserted estimate.

derivations.claim: Write $q(r)=r^2(1-r)^2$. Then $q'(r)=2r(1-r)(1-2r)$, so $q'(0)=q'(1)=0$, and $q''(0)=q''(1)=2$. Also $0\le q\le1/16$ on $[0,1]$. The constant and first two derivatives therefore match across the even-reflection and periodic seams; the extension is $C^2$, with bounded uniformly continuous derivatives. Since $h=q-1/30$, its values lie in $[-1/30,7/240]$, so $g\ge T_b-\epsilon/30>0$.

Expand $q(r)=r^2-2r^3+r^4$, so $\int_0^1q(r)\,dr=1/3-1/2+1/5=1/30$. Also $q(r)^2=r^4-4r^5+6r^6-4r^7+r^8$, whence
$$\int_0^1q(r)^2\,dr=\frac15-\frac46+\frac67-\frac48+\frac19=\frac1{630}.$$
Therefore $\int_0^1h(r)\,dr=0$ and
$$\int_0^1h(r)^2\,dr=\int_0^1(q-1/30)^2\,dr=\frac1{630}-\frac1{900}=\frac1{2100}.$$
Integrating over the other two coordinates now gives $\overline g=T_b$ and $E(0)=\epsilon^2L_2L_3L_1/2100=\epsilon^2|\Omega|/2100$.

The profile satisfies every initial-data hypothesis of [F1]; its vanishing normal derivative follows from $q'(0)=q'(1)=0$. Apply [F1] for existence and [F2] with the computed $E(0)$ to obtain the stated conserved mean and decay bound. This is a deduction within the adopted continuum model.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$ with $L_i>0$ metres, let $c>0$ be a constant volumetric heat capacity in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$ with $u'(T)=c$ throughout the range of $g$, let $k>0$ be a constant scalar conductivity in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ with $K\equiv kI_3$ in [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], and put $a=k/c$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$.

For $t>0$ define
$$T(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma(x-y,at)g(y)\,dy,\qquad \Gamma(z,\theta)=(4\pi\theta)^{-3/2}e^{-|z|^2/(4\theta)},$$
and set $T(x,0)=g(x)$ on $\overline\Omega$. This field is the unique $C^1$-in-time, $C^2$-in-space solution on each finite time interval of $c\partial_tT=k\Delta T$ on $\Omega$, with $\partial_nT=0$ on every face and the given initial value. It satisfies $T_{\min}\le T(x,t)\le T_{\max}$ for all $t\ge0$, has $C^2$ spatial derivatives continuous to $t=0$, and its right time derivative there is $a\Delta g$. Under [[post-td-local-energy-balance]] and [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], it is a global-in-time solution of that restricted physical continuum model.

derivations.claim: Inside the ball write $h(x)=1-|x-x_c|^2/r^2$, so $\phi=h^3$. On the sphere $h=0$, the first derivatives $3h^2\partial_i h$ and second derivatives $6h(\partial_i h)(\partial_j h)+3h^2\partial_i\partial_jh$ tend to zero; outside the ball they are zero. Hence $\phi$ is $C^2$ and nonnegative, and it is identically zero in a neighborhood of every face because $r<\frac12\min_iL_i$. The reflected periodic extension is therefore $C^2$, bounded, uniformly continuous with bounded derivatives, and positive on the original open ball.

The initial field $g=T_b+\epsilon\phi_{\rm per}$ is positive and satisfies the even-periodic compatibility hypotheses of [F1]. For $t>0$ and any $x\in\Omega$, the Gaussian $\Gamma(x-y,(k/c)t)$ is strictly positive on the ball. Choose a smaller closed ball on which the continuous $\phi_{\rm per}$ has a positive minimum; the Gaussian also has a positive minimum there. Its integral over that ball is positive, so the convolution in [F1] gives $T(x,t)-T_b>0$.

At $t=0$, $\phi_{\rm per}$ restricted to $\Omega$ vanishes outside $\overline B(x_c,r)$, a proper compact subset of the rectangle, while step 2.1 shows the positive-time perturbation is nonzero at every interior point. This is instantaneous support growth in the specified diffusion model only.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$, let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $z\notin E$. Then there are a nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^n$ and a real $c$ such that

$$\langle u,e\rangle\le c<\langle u,z\rangle\qquad(e\in E).$$

Thus an affine hyperplane strictly separates the point from the entire set.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: Choose affine coordinates identifying $H$ with $\mathbb R^k$. Convexity of $C$ makes its closure $K$ convex: approximate any two points of $K$ by sequences in $C$ and pass to the limit in each convex combination. Since $z\in\partial_H K$, choose $z_m\notin K$ with $z_m\to z$. By [F1], for each $m$ there are $u_m\ne0$ and $c_m$ with $u_m\cdot q\le c_m<u_m\cdot z_m$ for all $q\in K$. Normalize $u_m$ to unit length; [F3] places these vectors on the compact unit sphere, which is compact by [F2], so a subsequence converges to a unit vector $u$. [F2] and [F3] provide the convergent subsequence.

For every $q\in K$, the inequalities give $u_m\cdot(q-z_m)<0$. Along the convergent subsequence, continuity of the Euclidean inner product yields $u\cdot(q-z)\le0$. The limit vector has unit length, so its functional is nonzero and supports $K$, hence $C$, at $z$.

If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine hull $H$ of dimension at most $d-2$, its orthogonal complement has dimension at least two. Choose two nonparallel nonzero normals $n_1,n_2$ orthogonal to the direction space of $H$. For each $j$, the hyperplane $\{q:n_j\cdot(q-z)=0\}$ contains $H$ and therefore supports $C$ at $z$. The two hyperplanes are distinct because their normals are not parallel.

citations.quote:
Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the integral defining $h(t)=\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$ exists. Continuity of $f$ gives $h'(t)=f(t)$ on $(0,T)$: the difference quotient error is bounded by $\sup_{|s-t|\le|r|}|f(s)-f(t)|$, which tends to zero as $r\to0$. Also $h$ is continuous on $[0,T]$. The hypothesis gives $h'\le Lh$, so [F2]–[F3] yield $g'(t)\le0$ for $g(t)=e^{-Lt}h(t)$ on $(0,T)$. The mean value theorem makes $g$ nonincreasing; since $g(0)=0$ and $g\ge0$, $g\equiv0$ and $h\equiv0$.

For any $t>0$, the nonnegative continuous function $f$ has integral $h(t)=0$. If $f(t_0)>0$ at any $t_0>0$, continuity gives a positive lower bound on a nonempty subinterval of $[0,t_0]$, contradicting $h(t_0)=0$. citations.quote:
Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with a finite-valued slope map $P_i:\Gamma_i\to\mathbb R^{n_i}$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for every simple state $x$, the forward sector $A_x=\{y\in\Gamma_i:x\prec y\}$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$. For collinear $y=tx+(1-t)z$, $0<t<1$, $y\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$, and $x\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$.
Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], every forward sector $A_x$ has nonempty interior in its ambient simple domain $\Gamma_i$.

Let $C$ be a nonempty convex set in a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$ of dimension $k\ge1$, let $\operatorname{aff}C=H$, and put $K=\overline{C}^{\,H}$. If $z\in\partial_H K$ (that is, $z\in K$ and every relative neighborhood of $z$ meets $H\setminus K$), then there is a nonzero linear functional $\ell$ on the translation space of $H$ such that $\ell(q-z)\le0$ for all $q\in C$. If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine dimension at most $d-2$, then every $z\in C$ has at least two distinct ambient supporting hyperplanes containing $\operatorname{aff}C$.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be closed and convex with nonempty interior, $d\ge1$, and let $x\in\partial K$. Suppose $K$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$. Choose its inward unit normal $n$, so $n\cdot(q-x)\ge0$ for every $q\in K$. Then for every $v$ with $n\cdot v>0$, there is $\delta>0$ such that $x+tv\in\operatorname{int}K$ for every $0<t<\delta$.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be finite and convex, meaning $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for every $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$. For every $x_0\in U$, there are a neighborhood $V$ of $x_0$ and $L<\infty$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|$ for all $x,y\in V$. The same conclusion holds for finite concave functions by applying the result to $-f$.
Let $L\ge0$, $T>0$, and let $f:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous. If $f(t)\le L\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$ for every $t\in[0,T]$, then $f(t)=0$ for every $t\in[0,T]$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2\to0$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: For fixed $x=(u_x,v_x)$, the vertical section $I_x:=\{u:(u,v_x)\in A_x\}$ is a relatively closed convex interval by [F1]. The support plane at $x$ confines it to one side of $u_x$. Its inward normal has nonzero energy component, so [F4] gives a nontrivial interior vertical segment on that side.

The fiber orientation is locally constant in $v$. At any $x$, choose one vertical point just inside the supported half-space and one just outside; by [F4] the inside point can be chosen in $\operatorname{int}A_x$. Openness of $\Gamma_i$ and of the interior and exterior regions preserves these memberships on nearby fibers. Each such fiber therefore meets $\partial A_x$ between these two energy values. A support of $A_x$ at that boundary point also supports the point's own sector and so has its S2 orientation; the inside/outside placement fixes that orientation. Thus nearby fibers have the same sign as the fiber through $x$. Since $\Gamma_i$ is convex, it is connected; a locally constant two-valued sign is constant.

Let $u,w$ be two $C^1$ graph solutions of $Dq=-P_i(q,v)$ on a common open domain, and suppose $u(v_0)=w(v_0)$. Since $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz, choose a convex neighborhood of $(u(v_0),v_0)$ on which one Lipschitz constant $L$ works. Continuity of $u,w$ lets us choose a convex ball about $v_0$ whose closure lies in the common domain and whose two graph images stay in that neighborhood; take any $v$ in a smaller concentric ball. Put $d=v-v_0$ and $\gamma(t)=v_0+td$ for $0\le t\le1$. By [F8], $r(t)=u(\gamma(t))-w(\gamma(t))$ is $C^1$ and
$r'(t)=[-P_i(u(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))+P_i(w(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))]\cdot d.$
The local Lipschitz bound for $P_i$ gives $|r'(t)|\le L\|d\||r(t)|$. The derivative is continuous, hence integrable by [F10]; [F9] gives $r(t)=\int_0^t r'(s)\,ds$; hence $h(t):=|r(t)|\le L\|d\|\int_0^t h(s)\,ds$. Apply [F6] on $[0,1]$ to obtain $h=0$. Thus $u=w$ near $v_0$. Along any polygonal path in the common open domain, the set of path parameters at which equality holds is closed by continuity and open by this local result; since the path interval is connected and the set is nonempty, equality holds along the whole path. Every open connected subset of Euclidean space is polygonally connected: points reachable from a fixed point by finitely many segments in small balls form a nonempty relatively open and relatively closed set. Therefore equality extends throughout each common connected domain.

The convex, relatively closed interval $I_x$ contains a nontrivial segment on the inward side by step 1.1 and [F4]. Suppose it does not contain the whole open $\Gamma_i$-fiber on that side. Its endpoint $b$ toward that side then lies inside $\Gamma_i$; relative closedness puts $b$ in $I_x$, so the interval from $x$ to $b$ is a compact nondegenerate interval by [F7]. Let $x_1$ be its midpoint. Since $x_1\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_{x_1}\subseteq A_x$. The supporting plane of $A_{x_1}$ has nonzero energy coefficient, so its vertical section lies wholly on one side of $x_1$; being contained in $I_x$, it lies in one half of $[x,b]$ and has at most half its length. It is nonempty and closed relative to $[x,b]$, hence compact. Repeat: take the midpoint $x_{k+1}$ of the current compact interval $I_{x_k}$; then $x_k\prec x_{k+1}$, so the next section is nested inside the current one and again has at most half its length. These intervals have nonempty total intersection: otherwise their open complements would cover the first compact interval, a finite subcover would do so by [F7], and nesting would make one interval empty. Their lengths tend to zero, so the intersection has a unique point $x_\infty$, still in the first interval contained in $\Gamma_i$. The midpoint recursion and this unique intersection require no selection from an arbitrary countable family. Relative closedness puts $x_\infty$ in every $A_{x_k}$, hence $A_{x_\infty}\subseteq A_{x_k}$ by transitivity. Its vertical section is therefore only $\{x_\infty\}$, contradicting the nontrivial interior vertical segment at $x_\infty$ supplied by [F4]. Thus $I_x$ contains the whole open fiber on its inward side.

All states on a fixed work-coordinate fiber have the same orientation. If $x$ is oriented upward and a state $z$ above it were oriented downward, the full upward section from step 2.1 gives $x\prec z$, and the full downward section from $z$ gives $z\prec w$ for a state $w$ below $x$, contradicting the support at $x$. If a state $y$ below an upward $x$ were oriented downward, choose $z$ above $x$ with $x\prec z$; the first collinear implication in [F1], applied to $x$ between $y$ and $z$, gives $y\prec x$, contradicting the downward support at $y$. The reversed argument handles a downward $x$.
Adopt the coordinate convention $\varepsilon_i=1$. Step 2.1 and the common orientation give $x\prec y$ exactly for $u_y\ge u_x$ at fixed $v$, with strict comparison for $u_y>u_x$.

Put $\rho_x=\pi_v(\partial A_x)$. At a boundary point $z\in\partial A_x$, [F3] supplies a support to $A_x$. Because $A_z\subseteq A_x$, that plane also supports $A_z$ and equals its unique S2 plane. Its finite slope gives a nonvertical inward direction; [F4] supplies nearby vertical points inside $A_x$, while the opposite side is outside by the support. Neighborhoods of one inside and one outside point show every nearby work fiber meets $\partial A_x$. Hence $\rho_x$ is open. It is connected because S3 makes $\partial A_x$ arcwise connected and projection is continuous. By step 4.1, every vertical fiber over $\rho_x$ has exactly one boundary energy; call it $u_x(v)$.

For $v,v'\in\rho_x$, convexity of $A_x$ puts every convex combination of their boundary states in $A_x$. On any sufficiently small convex ball in $\rho_x$, the unique-boundary property and upward orientation make $u_x$ the least energy in each fiber. Therefore $u_x(tv+(1-t)v')\le t u_x(v)+(1-t)u_x(v')$, so $u_x$ is finite and convex there. It is locally Lipschitz by [F5]. The inward support at $(u_x(v),v)$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\ge -P_i(u_x(v),v)\cdot(v'-v).$
The support at $(u_x(v'),v')$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\le -P_i(u_x(v'),v')\cdot(v'-v).$
Local Lipschitz continuity of $u_x$ and $P_i$ makes the difference between these linear bounds $O(\|v'-v\|^2)$. Thus $u_x$ is differentiable with derivative $-P_i(u_x(v),v)$, and that derivative is locally Lipschitz. Hence $u_x\in C^1$ with locally Lipschitz derivative.

If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$. The boundary graphs agree at $v_y$ and solve the same differential equation. Fix an integer spatial dimension $d\geq1$, a reference length $\ell_0>0$ measured in metres, and a bounded Lebesgue-measurable region $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$ with dimensionless volume $V=|\Lambda|$. Its physical region is $\ell_0\Lambda$. The coordinate $x\in\Lambda$ is dimensionless and represents physical position $\ell_0x$. A finite positional configuration of $N$ classical point particles in $\Lambda$ is an unordered simple set $\omega=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subset\Lambda$; simple means that no point is repeated. Particle number $N$ is a dimensionless nonnegative integer and the physical number density corresponding to $N/V$ is $N/(\ell_0^dV)$.

A pair potential is an even measurable function $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where $\varphi(x)$ is the interaction energy in joules at physical displacement $\ell_0x$ and evenness means $\varphi(x)=\varphi(-x)$. Set $E_0=1\,\mathrm J$ and $\widehat\varphi=\varphi/E_0$. Whenever $\widehat\varphi$ is Borel measurable, it is the dimensionless numerical potential used by [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. For a labelled representative of $\omega$, define the positional pair energy
$$H_N(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\varphi(x_i-x_j),\qquad H_0=H_1=0.$$
If any pair is forbidden by the potential, its energy and hence $H_N$ are $+\infty$. This model contains no kinetic energy, internal molecular coordinates, quantum exchange terms, or external field.

The interaction is stable if there is a constant $B\geq0$, measured in joules, such that $H_N(\omega)\geq-BN$ for every finite simple configuration. It has a regular integrable tail if there are $R>0$ and a nonnegative nonincreasing measurable function $\psi:[R,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, measured in joules, such that $|\varphi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R$ and
$$\int_R^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)\,dr<\infty.$$
A stable potential with this tail condition is the stable regularly tempered class used for the free-cube results on this page. Superstability and a positive divergent core are stronger, separate hypotheses and are not implied by stability.

At temperature $T>0$ measured in kelvins, use the exact SI Boltzmann constant $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ of [[def-td-si-quantities]] and write $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ in joules inverse. Thus $\beta H_N$ is dimensionless. The activity $z>0$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity $\ell_0^{-d}$. A free-wall finite-volume model contains only positions in $\Lambda$ and uses $H_N$ above.

For periodic boundary conditions, identify a cubic cell of side $L$ in these dimensionless coordinates with the torus $\mathbb R^d/(L\mathbb Z^d)$. For its half-open representative $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$ and a finite simple configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$, define the periodic continuation $\omega^{\mathrm{per}}=\{x+Lk:x\in\omega,\ k\in\mathbb Z^d\}$ and
$$H_{L,\mathrm{per}}(\omega)=\frac12\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{\substack{y\in\omega^{\mathrm{per}}\\ y\ne x}}\varphi(y-x).$$
Here the inner sum omits only the identical point $y=x$; it includes images of the same particle in other cells. The factor $1/2$ removes double counting of ordered representatives of each periodic pair. For any fixed $L>0$ and finite $\omega$, the $|k|_\infty=m$ image shell has $O_d(m^{d-1})$ terms and, outside finitely many $m$, $|y-x+Lk|\geq (L/2)m$. Monotonicity and the finite weighted tail integral imply $\sum_m m^{d-1}\psi(Lm/2)<\infty$, so the far-image tail is absolutely convergent. The remaining near-image set is finite; a term $+\infty$ makes $H_{L,\mathrm{per}}=+\infty$, and otherwise the finite near terms plus the absolutely convergent tail define the sum. Translating a centered half-open cell to $[0,L)^d$ preserves every displacement and this energy. Free-wall and periodic preparations are distinct boundary conditions. All limits on this page concern positional configurations and do not by themselves include a momentum integral or a full phase-space energy shell.

$$A_n=\{\omega:N_{\Lambda_n}(\omega)/V_n\in D,\ H_{n,\mathrm{per}}(\omega)/(E_0V_n)\le\widehat e\},\qquad \widehat e=e/E_0.$$
Here $H_{n,\mathrm{per}}$ is the physical positional energy in joules in the same periodic convention; equivalently its event inequality is $H_{n,\mathrm{per}}/V_n\le e$. Assume AC and $T>0$, with $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$. Under the stable regularly tempered positional model of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]] and the adopted ensemble weights of [[post-td-equilibrium-ensemble-sampling]], assume the dimensionless potential $\widehat\varphi=\varphi/E_0$ is Borel measurable as required by the current mathematical carriers. Set $E_0=1\,\mathrm J$ and $\widehat\beta=E_0\beta$; write $F(\rho,\beta)$ and $P(\alpha,\beta)$ for the mathematical rates evaluated at $\widehat\beta$. Let $F(\rho,\beta)$ be the canonical log-partition rate per dimensionless reference volume, defined on interior attainable densities by the fixed-density limit and extended to the closed effective density domain by the upper-semicontinuous concave extension specified in [[thm-tdmath-canonical-grand-duality]]. Let
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\lim_{V\to\infty}V^{-1}\log\sum_{N\geq0}e^{\alpha N}Z(V,N),\qquad \alpha=\log z.$$
Then
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\{F(\rho,\beta)+\alpha\rho\},\qquad F(\rho,\beta)=\inf_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\{P(\alpha,\beta)-\alpha\rho\}.$$
In physical units, $p=(k_BT/\ell_0^d)P$ and the positional Helmholtz free-energy density is $f_{\mathrm{pos}}=-(k_BT/\ell_0^d)F$, with the fixed reference normalization of [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]]. This duality concerns limiting thermodynamic functions only. It does not imply local ensemble equivalence, uniqueness of a phase, or convergence at excluded density endpoints.

Assume AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, and HB as required by the current variational-pressure supplier. Let $E_0=1\,\mathrm J$, $\widehat\varphi=\varphi/E_0$, and assume $\widehat\varphi$ is Borel measurable. Require the exact superstable regular hypotheses of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]; use $\widehat H=H/E_0$ and $\widehat\beta=E_0\beta>0$ in its mathematical suppliers. Let $F(\rho,\beta)$ denote the numerical canonical rate evaluated at $\widehat\beta$; assume it is differentiable in physical $\beta$ at the chosen temperature and set $e=-\partial_\beta F(\rho,\beta)$, in joules per dimensionless reference volume. For periodic cubes $\Lambda_n$, take exact particle numbers $N_n$ with $N_n/V_n\to\rho$ at a positive interior attainable density. Choose a finite supporting activity parameter $\alpha$ for $F$ at $\rho$ and set $z=e^\alpha>0$; assume the corresponding stationary grand variational minimizer is the singleton $P^\ast$ as in [[post-td-grand-variational-phase-uniqueness]].

Then there exists a constructed sequence $\delta_n\downarrow0$ for which the periodic exact-$N_n$ canonical positional law, the periodic grand-canonical law at $(\alpha,\beta)$, and the uniform positional shell law of [[def-td-controlled-fixed-n-energy-shell]] on
$$N=N_n,\qquad |H_{L_n,\mathrm{per}}/V_n-e|\leq\delta_n,\qquad L_n=2n+1$$
all converge locally to $P^\ast$. Convergence means convergence of expectations for every measurable local observable $f$ supported in a bounded region and satisfying $|f|\leq c(1+N_A)$ there. The shell sequence is constructed from canonical concentration; arbitrary preassigned shrinking widths, exact zero-width surfaces, full phase-space shells involving kinetic momentum, and a conclusion at nonunique minimizers are not asserted.

Here local observables are evaluated on the periodic continuation of the prepared torus configuration. This is the same periodic boundary preparation, with no new physical sampling assumption; a configuration is not extended by the empty configuration outside its fundamental cube.

Assume AC, as required by the current mathematical definition and its shape suppliers. Let $d\geq2$, $E_0=1\,\mathrm J$, $\widehat\varphi=\varphi/E_0$, and assume $\widehat\varphi$ is Borel measurable and superstable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. Use $\widehat H=H/E_0$ and $\widehat\beta=E_0(k_BT)^{-1}>0$ in the mathematical rates. Let $(\Lambda_k)$ be a van Hove sequence as in [[def-td-admissible-van-hove-and-tempered-exterior]]. First, for free walls, the positional grand pressure along $\Lambda_k$ converges to the free-cube pressure of [[pthm-td-stable-tempered-free-cube-grand-pressure]]. For any positive interior attainable density $\rho$ and exact integers $N_k$ with $N_k/|\Lambda_k|\to\rho$, the exact-$N_k$ free-wall canonical log-partition rate converges to the same cube canonical rate. These two shape statements require superstability and regularity; stability alone is not asserted to suffice for arbitrary van Hove shapes.

Second, strengthen the potential hypothesis: for some $r_0>0$, $\widehat\varphi(x)\geq\widehat\chi(\|x\|_\infty)>0$ whenever $0<\|x\|_\infty\leq r_0$, where $\widehat\chi$ is nonincreasing and $\int_0^{r_0}\widehat\chi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr=+\infty$. For each fixed $t<\infty$, the free-wall grand pressure in $\Lambda_n$ with exterior $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$ then converges uniformly in $\zeta$ to the same free-cube pressure. The exterior interaction is the deterministic positional term of [[def-td-admissible-van-hove-and-tempered-exterior]], not a volume-filling external field. This genuine divergent-core condition is the exact stronger hypothesis of the current exterior supplier; it is not inferred from superstability or replaced by a weaker source condition.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer spatial dimension $d\geq 1$, a reference length $\ell_0>0$, and a bounded measurable region $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$ with dimensionless volume $V=|\Lambda|$. Its physical region is $\ell_0\Lambda$. A finite positional configuration of $N$ classical point particles in $\Lambda$ is an unordered simple set $\omega=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subset\Lambda$; simple means that no point is repeated. Particle number $N$ is a dimensionless nonnegative integer and the physical number density corresponding to $N/V$ is $N/(\ell_0^dV)$.

A pair potential is an even measurable function $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where $\varphi(x)$ is the interaction energy in joules at physical displacement $\ell_0x$ and evenness means $\varphi(x)=\varphi(-x)$. For a labelled representative of $\omega$, define the positional pair energy
$$H_N(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\varphi(x_i-x_j),\qquad H_0=H_1=0.$$
If any pair is forbidden by the potential, its energy and hence $H_N$ are $+\infty$. This model contains no kinetic energy, internal molecular coordinates, quantum exchange terms, or external field.

The interaction is stable if there is a constant $B\geq0$, measured in joules, such that $H_N(\omega)\geq-BN$ for every finite simple configuration. It has a regular integrable tail if there are $R>0$ and a nonnegative nonincreasing measurable function $\psi:[R,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, measured in joules, such that $|\varphi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R$ and
$$\int_R^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)\,dr<\infty.$$
A stable potential with this tail condition is the stable regularly tempered class used for the free-cube results on this page. Superstability and a positive divergent core are stronger, separate hypotheses and are not implied by stability.

At temperature $T>0$, write $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in joules inverse. The activity $z>0$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity $\ell_0^{-d}$. A free-wall finite-volume model contains only positions in $\Lambda$ and uses $H_N$ above. A periodic model uses the declared periodic cell and sums its periodic-image pair interactions with each unordered pair counted once. These are distinct boundary preparations. The limits on this page are positional configurational limits and do not by themselves include a momentum integral or a full phase-space energy shell.

Adopt the unlabelled positional configuration measure $\mu_{\Lambda,N}$ obtained from labelled tuples by dividing by permutation multiplicity. Thus, for every nonnegative measurable symmetric function $f$ on $\Lambda^N$,
$$\int f(\omega)\,\mu_{\Lambda,N}(d\omega)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda^N}f(\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\})\,d^{dN}x.$$
The reference coordinates and length scale are those of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. This convention treats two labelled lists that differ only by a particle permutation as the same positional state. The factor $1/N!$ is an adopted indistinguishable-particle measure convention for this classical model, not a theorem that classical trajectories or every classical description must use quotient states.

For later comparison, define the unit-intensity Poisson reference on a finite region by
$$Q_\Lambda(d\omega)=e^{-|\Lambda|}\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}\mu_{\Lambda,N}(d\omega).$$
Its total mass is one because $\mu_{\Lambda,N}$ has total mass $|\Lambda|^N/N!$ and $e^{-|\Lambda|}\sum_{N\geq0}|\Lambda|^N/N!=1$. This is a positional reference measure in the chosen dimensionless coordinates; it supplies no empirical claim about particle trajectories.

For a specified finite region and boundary preparation, take $T>0$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, and the positional energy in [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. For each fixed $N$, specialize the measurable-model canonical preparation of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] to the dimensionless positional configuration measure $\mu_{\Lambda,N}$; adopt the law
$$P_{\Lambda,N}^{\mathrm{can}}(d\omega)=Z_{\Lambda,N}^{-1}e^{-\beta H_N(\omega)}\mu_{\Lambda,N}(d\omega),\qquad Z_{\Lambda,N}=\int e^{-\beta H_N}\,d\mu_{\Lambda,N},$$
whenever $0<Z_{\Lambda,N}<\infty$. Separately adopt the grand-canonical law at activity $z>0$ to have weights $z^{N(\omega)}e^{-\beta H_{N(\omega)}(\omega)}$ relative to the same indistinguishable positional measures; its normalizer is $\Xi_\Lambda(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{\Lambda,N}$ when finite. Here $z$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity in [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]], and $\alpha=\log z$.

For the controlled positional shell of [[def-td-controlled-fixed-n-energy-shell]], adopt the conditional measure $M_n$ only when its shell has positive finite reference measure. These are probability-law preparations used to define the model. They are not derived from Hamiltonian trajectories, and they do not assert that a laboratory apparatus reaches any of them. The inverse-temperature-zero hard-core continuation is governed separately by [[def-td-retained-hard-core-zero-beta-preparation]].

derivations.claim: The allowed labelled pairs form two disjoint triangles, $x_2\geq x_1+a$ and $x_1\geq x_2+a$. The first has area $\int_0^{L-a}(L-a-x_1)\,dx_1=(L-a)^2/2$, and the second has the same area by exchanging coordinates.

Their total allowed area is $(L-a)^2$. On it $e^{-\beta H_2}=1$; on the excluded band it is zero because $H_2=+\infty$. Multiplying the allowed area by the measure factor $1/2$ from [A1] gives $Z_{\Lambda,2}=(L-a)^2/2$, as asserted.

case_scope.source_excerpt: For the ideal positional gas $\varphi=0$ in a region of dimensionless volume $V$, the grand partition is $\Xi_V(z,\beta)=e^{zV}$. Now impose an external energy $c$ joules per particle at every point of the volume. The new grand partition is $\Xi_V^{(c)}=e^{ze^{-\beta c}V}$, so the dimensionless pressure rate changes from $z$ to $ze^{-\beta c}$ when $c\neq0$. This exact volume-filling external preparation is not a member of the deterministic exterior class used by [[pthm-td-qualified-van-hove-and-exterior-limit]].
